turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: PM Designer thriving. I also just think generally the AI job apocalypse is not really a thing. Absolutely we see companies starting to reorganize and I think that makes a lot of sense. I think to be honest, a lot of the reorganization, you can say it's AI, but it's like we overhired and the company's not doing as well and all that kind of ... It was coming and this is a good excuse. But the mass unemployment thing I think that some AI CEOs are talking about, I think that's not going to happen. The pattern that I see so far, and again, I don't have a total crystal ball, but I do feel like we've seen enough of the new model drops to have some sense of how this is going is that what a new model drop does or what models do in general is they make yesterday's human competence cheap. (01:13:56): So what I mean by that is they ingest all this data of what has happened already and they make it really cheap to deploy that in whatever situation you want as your own. (01:14:10): And what happens then is this is a new power that everyone has, so it gets adopted super rapidly and suddenly that stuff is everywhere. It's suddenly anyone can make a landing page. There's new landing pages everywhere. Suddenly everyone can write. There's slop tweets everywhere. But what's interesting is because it's all coming from these models and everyone's using basically the same models, it all looks the same if you use it in the most default basic way. And so it becomes commoditized. It's not valuable anymore. (01:14:50): And what humans do is we sort of go in there, and we're like, "Yeah," we have all this frozen human competence from yesterday. How do I use this to make something new and interesting? And I really think that structurally because of the way the models work, because of the financial incentives of model companies to make them compliant and aligned, structurally they're always going to be trailing behind those people who are taking the models and using them to make new expertise or make new things that haven't been done that way before for their very, very particular situation. And that stuff is going to get incorporated into the models, but again, it will create room for people to push further ahead. (01:15:34): And I think that you see this in a small way in pretty much all the jobs is engineers. Suddenly everyone's an engineer, but that doesn't mean we fire the engineers. There's way more demand for engineers because you need the engineers to figure out, okay, this is all slop. How should this actually go in our code base? And I think that's something that the benchmarks rising doesn't really capture and it feels like a thing that will take a long time to change.
turns.zh: PM 设计师蓬勃发展。我还认为，一般来说，人工智能工作启示录并不是真正的事情。当然，我们看到公司开始重组，我认为这很有意义。我认为说实话，很多重组，你可以说是人工智能，但就像我们过度雇用而公司表现不佳之类的......它即将到来，这是一个很好的借口。但我认为一些人工智能首席执行官正在谈论的大规模失业问题，我认为这不会发生。到目前为止，我看到的模式，再说一次，我没有一个完整的水晶球，但我确实觉得我们已经看到了足够多的新模型下降，对事情的进展有一定的了解，即新模型下降的作用或一般模型的作用是它们使昨天的人类能力变得廉价。 (01:13:56)：所以我的意思是，他们吸收了已经发生的所有这些数据，并且在你想要的任何情况下部署这些数据变得非常便宜。 (01:14:10)：然后发生的事情是，这是每个人都拥有的新力量，因此它被迅速采用，突然之间，这种东西无处不在。突然之间，任何人都可以制作登陆页面。到处都有新的登陆页面。突然间每个人都可以写作。到处都是垃圾推文。但有趣的是，因为它都来自这些模型，而且每个人都使用基本相同的模型，如果您以最默认的基本方式使用它，它看起来都一样。因此它变得商品化。它已经不值钱了。 (01:14:50)：人类所做的就是我们进入那里，我们会说，“是的”，我们从昨天起就拥有了所有这些冻结的人类能力。我如何利用它来创造一些新的、有趣的东西？我真的认为，从结构上讲，由于模型的工作方式，由于模型公司的财务激励措施，使模型合规和一致，从结构上讲，他们总是会落后于那些采用模型并利用模型来获得新专业知识或创造新事物的人，这些人以前在非常非常特殊的情况下没有这样做过。这些东西将被纳入模型中，但同样，它将为人们进一步前进创造空间。 (01:15:34)：我认为你在几乎所有的工作都是工程师中都看到了这一点。突然间每个人都是工程师，但这并不意味着我们解雇工程师。对工程师的需求要大得多，因为你需要工程师弄清楚，好吧，这都是废话。这在我们的代码库中实际上应该如何进行？我认为基准的上升并没有真正体现这一点，而且感觉需要很长时间才能改变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People may be hearing in this prediction here of just, okay, the job apocalypse not going to, people are not going to be all fired. There's going to be human jobs remaining for quite a while. It may be almost too comforting because you probably have to change the way you operate to still have a job in the future. Do you have any sense of just like, here's what you need to do to not be one of these layoffs?
turns.zh: 人们可能会在这里听到这样的预测：好吧，工作末日不会发生，人们不会全部被解雇。人类的工作岗位将会保留相当长一段时间。这可能太令人欣慰了，因为你可能必须改变你的运作方式才能在未来保住工作。您是否有这样的感觉：您需要采取以下措施才能不成为这些裁员中的一员？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yes. And I think that is actually super important. The only thing you need to do is ride the models and that means use them for whatever it is that you do. We've talked about how Codex and Cowork are becoming the sort of standard operating system for work. If you're just doing that and when new models come out, you're trying them and figuring out, okay, now there are new powers. How can I use them? Instead of just being like, "I'm going to try to ignore it because it makes me afraid." Which I think is honestly, it's rational. It's a reasonable response. (01:16:56): And also if you ride on top of them, they extend your powers in a way that doesn't leave you behind. You're part of the future and part of the way work happens. And I think that we're going to need people doing that for a very, very long time.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为这实际上非常重要。您唯一需要做的就是驾驶模型，这意味着无论您做什么，都可以使用它们。我们已经讨论了 Codex 和 Cowork 如何成为一种标准的工作操作系统。如果你只是这样做，当新模型出现时，你正在尝试它们并弄清楚，好吧，现在有了新的能力。我该如何使用它们？而不是只是说“我要尝试忽略它，因为它让我害怕。”老实说，我认为这是合理的。这是一个合理的回应。 (01:16:56)：而且，如果你骑在它们上面，它们会以一种不会让你落后的方式扩展你的力量。您是未来的一部分，也是工作方式的一部分。我认为我们将需要人们在很长一段时间内这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like this term, ride the model. So what's like say a new model comes out, what do you think someone say working at, I don't know, Salesforce? Say a PM at Salesforce, what should they do to ride the model?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个词，骑模型。那么，就像说一种新模型出现一样，你认为在 Salesforce 工作的人会说什么呢？我不知道？ Salesforce 的 PM 说，他们应该怎么做才能使用该模型？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Well, one of the things that's really interesting is a lot of companies handicap their employees from even doing this because I don't know if you can use the latest models at Salesforce. A lot of times you have to wait or it's whatever. So maybe you have to do it in your off time. But the thing that I really like to do with new models is play, and there are certain things where I know it can't quite do it yet, but when a new model comes out, I always turn the rock over again to be like, "Can I do it now?" So it could not do the senior engineer benchmark last time, and I turned the rock over again and now it's at a 60 out of 100, which is really good. So the way to ride the models is not one specific thing because they're always changing, but it is to be curious and playful to apply the model, the new model to whatever it is that you care about, whether that's your job or something outside of your job and to keep turning over rocks because it may not work now, but it may work eventually. (01:18:33): It probably will work eventually and the way that you use it matters. So what's really cool is that I think people think of the edge of AI as being in San Francisco, and I actually don't think that that's where it is. I think the edge of AI is wherever AI meets a real human doing something because the people at San Francisco, they're making it, but they don't actually know a lot about how to use it. They don't know, or at least they don't know everything about how to use it. They need to see how other people use it. (01:19:02): And so whenever a new model comes out, you get to be one of the first people in the world to discover what it might be useful for. And it's like a new discovery. And I think that's why, for example, we're in Brooklyn, but I really think of us, and I think we are quite far ahead of people in San Francisco because we just use them for everything. And if people do that consistently, I think it's going to be very hard to lose.
turns.zh: 嗯，真正有趣的事情之一是很多公司甚至阻碍他们的员工这样做，因为我不知道你是否可以使用 Salesforce 的最新模型。很多时候你必须等待，或者其他什么。所以也许你必须在休息时间做这件事。但我真正喜欢用新模型做的事情是玩，有些事情我知道它还不能完全做到，但当新模型出现时，我总是会再次把石头翻过来，就像，“我现在可以做吗？”所以上次它无法完成高级工程师基准测试，我又把石头翻过来，现在它是 60 分（满分 100 分），这真的很好。因此，驾驭模型的方式并不是一件具体的事情，因为它们总是在变化，而是带着好奇和有趣的态度，将模型、新模型应用到你关心的任何事物上，无论那是你的工作还是工作之外的东西，并不断翻滚石头，因为它现在可能行不通，但最终可能行得通。 (01:18:33)：它最终可能会发挥作用，并且使用它的方式很重要。所以真正酷的是，我认为人们认为人工智能的边缘在旧金山，但我实际上并不认为那是它所在的地方。我认为人工智能的边缘是人工智能遇到真正的人类做某事的地方，因为旧金山的人们正在制造它，但他们实际上并不知道如何使用它。他们不知道，或者至少不知道如何使用它。他们需要看看其他人如何使用它。 (01:19:02)：因此，每当新模型出现时，您都会成为世界上第一批发现它可能有用的人之一。这就像一个新发现。我认为这就是为什么，例如，我们在布鲁克林，但我真的很想我们，而且我认为我们远远领先于旧金山的人，因为我们只是将它们用于所有事情。如果人们始终如一地这样做，我认为输球就很难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is one of the most amazing things about AI right now is no matter how much money you have or a little money you have, you have access to the most advanced AI model. It's not free, so you need some money and you can get it immediately when it comes out. Maybe the only people that have an advantage are the people working at OpenAI or Anthropic, but otherwise it's just available.
turns.zh: 现在人工智能最令人惊奇的事情之一是，无论你有多少钱或有多少钱，你都可以获得最先进的人工智能模型。它不是免费的，所以你需要一些钱，当它出来时你可以立即得到它。也许唯一有优势的人是在 OpenAI 或 Anthropic 工作的人，但除此之外，它只是可用的。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I know. I was at their event with you, their Code with Claude event with you last week or a couple weeks ago and they're all using mythos and I'm like, "God, damn it." It's so annoying, but I think that's totally true. If IBM had invented AI, you can bet it would not be like this, and it would be a bajillion dollars and only the top companies could use it and they would be using it in the weirdest, most uninteresting ways. It's really important that AI was built in America and in the Silicon Valley culture that's like, "We want to make intelligence too cheap to meter." That's not the default stance. And it means that everyone has this broadly accessible tool that they can use and I think that's amazing.
turns.zh: 我知道。上周或几周前我和你一起参加了他们的 Code with Claude 活动，他们都在使用神话，我当时想，“上帝，该死的。”这太烦人了，但我认为这是完全正确的。如果 IBM 发明了人工智能，你可以打赌它不会是这样的，这将是数以亿计的美元，只有顶级公司才能使用它，而且他们会以最奇怪、最无趣的方式使用它。人工智能是在美国和硅谷文化中构建的，这一点非常重要，就像“我们希望让智能变得便宜到无法计量”。这不是默认立场。这意味着每个人都可以使用这个广泛使用的工具，我认为这太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good point. And interestingly, it's also created the most fastest growing companies in history, the biggest companies in history.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的观点。有趣的是，它还创造了历史上增长最快的公司、历史上最大的公司。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: That's true. Those Silicon Valley guys, they're smart.
turns.zh: 这是真的。那些硅谷人，他们很聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If I zoom out on the conversation, it's really interesting. There's kind of these two sides to the coin. One is not a lot is actually, so much is not changing. SaaS continues, jobs not disappearing. We're still emailing each other. We're still working on Slack. A lot of the work not changed. On the other hand, every role transformed, engineers don't write code, PMs don't write PRDs, design and design. It's so interesting how much has changed, how much has not changed. I don't know. It's interesting that people think it's going to be this whole new world, but in many ways it's, okay, it'll continue the way it is with a lot of stuff around the edges.
turns.zh: 如果我把谈话缩小，那真的很有趣。硬币有两个方面。其实并不是很多，很多都没有改变。 SaaS 仍在继续，工作岗位并没有消失。我们仍然互相发送电子邮件。我们仍在研究 Slack。很多工作没有改变。另一方面，每一个角色的转变，工程师不写代码，PM不写PRD，设计还是设计。有趣的是，有多少改变了，有多少没有改变。我不知道。有趣的是，人们认为这将是一个全新的世界，但在很多方面，好吧，它会继续现状，但有很多边缘的东西。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: That's how I feel. I'm simultaneously so excited and it feels like everything has changed, and I'm so bullish on it and the progress that we're making, all that kind of stuff. And, yeah, I feel like there are these things where they're going to be pretty similar to how they are and that's probably good. And I think generally our intuitions about the future, the model that I have of what our intuitions are about the future is the intuitions that people had in the Middle Ages about what happened at the end of the horizon. It's like, are there dragons? Does it drop off into nothingness or whatever? A lot of people have a lot of deep intuition that there's something terrible going to happen over the horizon and also that some people are like, "There's something incredible. It's going to change everything. We're all going to be happy. It's a utopia." (01:22:28): And what happens is you get there and you're like, there's some really cool things, there's some not cool things and it's just another horizon. And I think that's the way to think about the future. And until you get to that place where you're starting to see it, and I think we get to see it because we get to see it internally all the time. It's important not to let your mind get away from you and being like, "This is going to happen and this is going to happen and whatever." Because you're going to tell a story that sounds so real in the moment, but later on you're like, "Actually it's much more complex than that." And somewhere it's sort of a both, everything's changed and nothing has. And once you get there, I think you're sort of starting to see like, "Oh, yeah, this is a real thing."
turns.zh: 我就是这样的感觉。我同时感到非常兴奋，感觉一切都改变了，我非常看好它以及我们正在取得的进展，所有这些东西。是的，我觉得有些东西会与它们本来的样子非常相似，这可能很好。我认为一般来说我们对未来的直觉，我对未来直觉的模型是中世纪人们对地平线尽头发生的事情的直觉。就像，有龙吗？它会陷入虚无还是其他什么？很多人有很多深刻的直觉，认为地平线上将会发生一些可怕的事情，而且有些人会说，“有一些令人难以置信的事情。它将改变一切。我们都会幸福的。这是一个乌托邦。” (01:22:28)：当你到达那里时，你会觉得，有一些非常酷的东西，也有一些不酷的东西，这只是另一个地平线。我认为这就是思考未来的方式。直到你到达那个地方，你开始看到它，我想我们会看到它，因为我们一直在内部看到它。重要的是不要让你的思绪离开你，并说“这将会发生，这将会发生，等等。”因为你要讲的故事当时听起来很真实，但后来你会想，“实际上比这复杂得多。”在某些地方，两者兼而有之，一切都变了，但又什么都没有。一旦你到达那里，我想你就会开始看到，“哦，是的，这是真的。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Part of it is the AI companies are very good at scaring us about what might happen in the future. And I think that's actually shifting. I think they've realized maybe we should not freak everybody out about the dangers.
turns.zh: 部分原因是人工智能公司非常擅长用未来可能发生的事情来吓唬我们。我认为这种情况实际上正在发生变化。我认为他们已经意识到也许我们不应该让每个人都对危险感到害怕。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: That PR strategy just does not make any sense to me. I do think that it's genuine, but it's so ineffective, and I think it's also wrong.
turns.zh: 这种公关策略对我来说没有任何意义。我确实认为它是真实的，但它是如此无效，而且我认为它也是错误的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How about we end with maybe just a few things listeners should do to be successful over the next year with the way the world is moving.
turns.zh: 我们不妨以听众应该做的几件事作为结尾，以便在明年跟随世界的发展方式取得成功。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Ride the models. I would try all of your workflows in Codex or Cowork and see how that works. And if your company doesn't let you do it on your own time, I would try out some of these agent products like OpenClaw or Hermes or for less technical people, there's like Victor, we have OnePlus ones. I would get comfortable with both of those ways of working and try to have fun. I think there's too much of I'm doing this because I have FOMO, I might lose my job or I might miss out on this big thing or whatever. And the best way to actually figure out interesting, useful things to do with AI is to do something enjoyable.
turns.zh: 骑模型。我会在 Codex 或 Cowork 中尝试你们的所有工作流程，看看它是如何工作的。如果你的公司不允许你在自己​​的时间里做这件事，我会尝试一些代理产品，比如 OpenClaw 或 Hermes，或者对于技术含量较低的人来说，比如 Victor，我们有 OnePlus 的产品。我会适应这两种工作方式并尝试从中获得乐趣。我认为我这样做的太多原因是因为我有 FOMO，我可能会失去工作，或者我可能会错过这件大事或其他什么。真正弄清楚人工智能有趣、有用的事情的最好方法就是做一些令人愉快的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nikhil Singal was on the podcast and the way he described it is you got to find your moment of joy with AI once you find like, "Wow, I can't believe AI did this for me. This is awesome. We're going to keep building stuff."
turns.zh: Nikhil Singal 在播客中，他描述的方式是，一旦你发现“哇，我不敢相信人工智能为我做了这件事。这太棒了。我们将继续创造东西”，你就必须找到人工智能带来的快乐时刻。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah, I agree.
turns.zh: 是的，我同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So if you haven't seen that yet, then it's just like, try, fine, try solving it. The thing I hear a lot is just find a problem in your life or work and see if AI can do it. Go to Lovable, go to apply code, go to Replit, just try to build the thing and often it's like, holy shit, this is so cool." (01:24:58): Dan, is there anything else that we haven't covered? We've gone deep on so much. Is there anything else you wanted to share? Anything else you want to predict or just say before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 因此，如果您还没有看到这一点，那么就像，尝试，好吧，尝试解决它。我经常听到的一句话是，找到你生活或工作中的问题，看看人工智能是否能做到。去 Lovable，去应用代码，去 Replit，只是尝试构建这个东西，通常会感觉，天啊，这太酷了。” (01:24:58)：Dan，还有什么我们没有提到的吗？我们已经深入了这么多。还有什么你想分享的吗？在我们进入非常激动人心的闪电回合之前，你还有什么想预测或想说的吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I think we covered it. We did a lot. This is awesome, and I'm very excited to see how well or poorly I do in a year, and I hope that you hold me to it.
turns.zh: 我想我们已经涵盖了。我们做了很多。 This is awesome, and I'm very excited to see how well or poorly I do in a year, and I hope that you hold me to it.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to have AI score us. How about that?
turns.zh: 我们将让人工智能为我们评分。怎么样？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 伟大的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Look at the world like a dance prediction. See where it goes. Well, with that, Dan Shipper, we've reached a very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 像舞蹈预测一样看待世界。看看它去哪里了。好吧，丹·希珀，我们已经进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 您发现自己最向其他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Obviously Annie Dillard. Everyone at every has to read The Writing Life. When you join, you get a copy and you have to read it. You only have to read the last chapter though. I think the last chapter is incredible, and it is at the intersection of writing and technology and the future and its relationship to the future and to time. It's everything about every wrapped up into a very tight chapter. It's so good. And I think Annie Dillard just generally is fantastic. (01:26:11): What else do I recommend? I'll just tell you a couple things that I've read that I've really liked recently, and whenever I like something, I always just tell everyone about it. So I have recommended these a lot. I've been reading... One of the things I learned, which I didn't know is Churchill is a really good writer and he has a whole history of World War II that he wrote and it's like a combination history and memoir. And I think that's so cool because he was there, he did it. And there's something about what we do at everywhere. I feel some sort of kinship with that of like we're building stuff, we're writing stuff and it's very rare to find people that also do that. (01:26:48): And so Churchill History of World War II is fantastic. I just finished the first volume. I'm on the second volume. The Nazis just invaded France. It's very captivating stuff. So that's one. I've been on a little bit of a quantum physics kick recently. AI is actually very good for quantum physics if you get into it. And there's this book called The Rigor of Angels that I just finished, which is, it's a history of ideas that relates Heisenberg, who has his uncertainty principle. Borges, who's an Argentinian fiction writer, wrote a bunch of great short stories. They're actually starting to get a lot of play now because they're very AI related. And Cont and very cool, super mind-blowing. Lots of interesting overlaps with AI stuff and, yeah, highly recommend.
turns.zh: 显然是安妮·迪拉德。每个人都必须阅读《写作生活》。当你加入时，你会得到一份副本，你必须阅读它。不过你只需要阅读最后一章。我认为最后一章令人难以置信，它是写作、技术、未来及其与未来和时间的关系的交叉点。所有的一切都被包裹在一个非常紧凑的章节中。太好了。我认为安妮·迪拉德总的来说非常棒。 (01:26:11)：我还有什么建议？我只想告诉你一些我最近读过的、我非常喜欢的东西，每当我喜欢什么东西时，我总是会告诉大家。所以我推荐了很多这些。我一直在读……我学到的一件事（我不知道）是丘吉尔是一位非常优秀的作家，他写了一部完整的二战历史，就像一本历史和回忆录的结合体。我认为这太酷了，因为他在那里，他做到了。我们在任何地方所做的事情都是有道理的。我觉得与我们正在构建东西、我们正在编写东西有某种相似之处，但很少有人也这样做。 (01:26:48)：丘吉尔的二战史非常棒。我刚刚完成第一卷。我已经在看第二卷了纳粹刚刚入侵法国。这是非常迷人的东西。这就是其中之一。我最近对量子物理有点感兴趣。如果你深入研究人工智能，它实际上对量子物理学非常有利。我刚刚读完这本书，叫《天使的严密》，这是一本关于海森堡的思想史，海森堡有他的不确定性原理。博尔赫斯是一位阿根廷小说家，写了很多精彩的短篇小说。事实上，它们现在已经开始得到广泛应用，因为它们与人工智能密切相关。继续，非常酷，超级令人兴奋。与人工智能的东西有很多有趣的重叠，是的，强烈推荐。

turns.en: Yes, I have several. The core one that I wrote for myself in college was do things worth writing about and write things worth reading. And I've listened to so many of his talks and there's this one talk that he gives where it's just one sentence, but he just talks about when you're dealing with stuff that's hard, what you want to do is be able to relate to it from a position of spaciousness and strength. (01:30:13): And there is something I think really interesting and important in that. A lot of the meditation discourse are just generally like, how do you deal with hard things? It's a little bit more of the David Goggins. (01:30:24): You just got to go for it kind of. And sometimes that can work. And if not, can I get there because it will be much more productive for me to deal with it from that place." And that has been very, very helpful for me.
turns.zh: 是的，我有几个。我在大学时为自己写的核心内容是做值得写的事情，写值得读的事情。还有一个人，Rob Burbea，他在人工智能冥想重叠话语中非常受欢迎，这也是一件大事，我也是，我真的很喜欢他。他死了，但我认为他很了不起。我听过他的很多演讲，其中有一次他只讲了一句话，但他只是谈到，当你处理困难的事情时，你想做的是能够从一种宽广和力量的角度来处理它。 (01:30:13)：我认为其中有一些非常有趣且重要的事情。很多冥想的讨论都是笼统地说，你如何处理困难的事情？这更像是大卫·戈金斯的风格。 (01:30:24)：你必须全力以赴。有时这会起作用。而且我认为有时当你处理事情时，例如，当你处理事情时，我非常担心人工智能将如何改变我的工作，这对我很有帮助，“我是从宽敞和力量的有利角度来处理这个问题的吗？如果没有，我可以到达那里，因为从那个地方处理它对我来说会更有效率。”这对我来说非常非常有帮助。
